The Cloudflare Worker verifies every bullet it emits against the strings in this file, so nothing reaches a page that isn't approved here. Add a variant here before the tailor can ever use it.

dissertation.title: Money Can't Buy Happiness: Social Capital & Life Satisfaction
dissertation.fullTitle: Money can't buy happiness: The cross-cultural relationships between social capital and life satisfaction
dissertation.institution: City St George's, University of London
short: Analysed 11,249 people in five countries (ISSP 2017, OLS in R): does social connection go with happier lives?
Trust in fair institutions predicted satisfaction most consistently; relative income had no significant effect.
Social capital mattered most where governments did least, shifting with culture and natural-disaster risk.
dissertation._note: short = the condensed version on every CV and on commercial (track A) tailored CVs. bullets = the full research version, used on research-track (track B) tailored CVs.
bullets: Modelled the link between social capital and life satisfaction across five countries in R, using the International Social Survey Programme (ISSP) 2017 module (n = 11,249) as one instrument for all three of Putnam's dimensions.
Methods: multiple imputation (MICE), PCA-built constructs, country-level and pooled OLS with interaction terms, Tukey pairwise comparisons, and AIC/BIC model comparison.

Perceived institutional fairness was the most consistent cross-cultural predictor of life satisfaction. Relative income (within-country brackets) had no significant main effect, but as income rose, the links between life satisfaction and trust, daily contact and organisational contact weakened.

Social capital mattered more where state capacity was weaker (lower human development, fewer government resources, more corruption), while better governance had its own positive effect on life satisfaction.
Made policy recommendations on institutional transparency, civic infrastructure and bridging social capital.

project.title: What Wins on Grass: Wimbledon Monte Carlo Match Simulator
project.label: Independent project
short: Built with Claude Code: a Python and JavaScript app that gives every player in the Wimbledon men's draw a fingerprint from IBM Slam Tracker point data (2011–2023), shown as interactive charts.
Matchups are played out point by point from two fingerprints, not regressed: 68.4% accurate on 827 matches.
bullets: Built with Claude Code as a Python data pipeline and a browser app: a fingerprint for every player in the Wimbledon men's draw from IBM Slam Tracker point-by-point data (2011–2023), about 48,000 points a season.
Each fingerprint covers serve, return and under-pressure play (how unpredictably a player serves, holds at break point and fades across sets), weighted by recency and opponent quality.
Every player has a page of interactive charts (serve speed and direction, rally length, pressure play, match log) and a place on a leaderboard.

Matchups are simulated, not regressed: two fingerprints play a match out point by point, 25,000 times in the browser, through a serve, rally and pressure model, then calibrated. Backtested on 827 matches (2014–2023), each season predicted only from earlier ones: 68.4% accurate.

_layout._note: Read by scripts/build_cv.py and cv-ats.html. page1Roles = roles before "Experience (continued)". omit = bullets the designed CV drops to hold two A4 pages (role-bullet id, or "research:<opening words>"). eduResultInMeta = set each degree's result on its school | dates line (designed CV only). atsOmit = like omit, for the ATS export, which only cuts if it runs over itself.

_README_ats: Experience entries are two lines: the job title alone (specialism after a comma), then 'Company | City, Country | Dates'. Client names live in the bullets, never in a title line, so parsers take the company from line 2. education[].degreeAts is the ATS form of a degree.
